rows: Appears to diverge from virtual focus

questions.question: Q1. State the lens formula and sign convention.
questions.answer: For a thin lens: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (Cartesian sign convention). Distances measured from the optical centre: object distance u negative if on the incident side; f positive for a convex (converging) lens, negative for a concave (diverging) lens.

questions.question: Q2. Write the lensmaker's formula and explain its terms.
questions.answer: 1/f = (n−1)[1/R₁ − 1/R₂], where n is the relative refractive index and R₁, R₂ are the radii of curvature of the two surfaces (positive/negative per sign convention). It links focal length to material and curvature.
questions.shortcut: 1/f = (n−1)(1/R₁−1/R₂); more curved or higher n → shorter f.
questions.example: A biconvex lens with R₁=+R, R₂=−R gives 1/f = 2(n−1)/R.

questions.question: Q3. Define the power of a lens and its SI unit.
questions.answer: Power P = 1/f (f in metres), measured in dioptres (D). For convex P>0, for concave P<0. The power of two thin lenses in contact adds: P_total = P₁ + P₂.
questions.shortcut: P = 1/f(m); in D; add powers for thin-lens combinations.
questions.example: A 20 cm convex lens → P = +5 D.

questions.question: Q4. Find the focal length and power of a double-convex lens with R₁ = R₂ = 20 cm, n = 1.5.
Q5. Explain a magnifying glass (simple microscope) and angular magnification M = 1 + D/f.
questions.answer: A simple microscope (magnifying glass) holds an object within the near-point focal distance f, producing a virtual erect image at the near-point D. The angular magnification is M = D/f (image at infinity) or M = 1 + D/f (image at the near-point D = 25 cm).
questions.shortcut: M = 1 + D/f for near-point viewing; D/f for infinity.

questions.question: Q6. A compound microscope with objective f_o = 0.5 cm and eyepiece f_e = 2 cm. Estimate magnification when image at infinity.
questions.answer: For an image at infinity, M ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e), with L ≈ 15 cm tube length, D = 25 cm: M ≈ (15/0.5)(25/2) = 30×12.5 = 375×.

questions.question: Q7. Define magnification of a lens and state its sign convention.
questions.answer: Linear magnification m = h'/h = −v/u. A negative m means the image is inverted; positive m means it is erect. The magnitude |m| is the size ratio image/object.
questions.example: An object at 2f gives m = −1 (same size, inverted).

questions.question: Q8. Find the image position for an object 15 cm in front of a convex lens of f = 10 cm.
questions.answer: Use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (magnitudes, convex lens): 1/v = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm (real, on the opposite side). Magnification m = v/u = 30/15 = 2, so the image is real, inverted and 2× the object size.
questions.shortcut: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u ; m = v/u. Object between f and 2f gives an image beyond 2f, magnified.
questions.example: Image 30 cm from the lens, m = −2 (inverted, 2×).

questions.question: Q9. How do you find the combined power of two thin lenses in contact?
questions.answer: The powers simply add: P_total = P₁ + P₂ (each P = 1/f in metres). This is the basis of correcting the eye's vision with spectacle lenses of the right total power.
questions.example: +4 D and −1 D in contact give +3 D.

questions.question: Q10. Explain why a concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.
questions.answer: A concave (diverging) lens spreads rays; the refracted rays diverge and never actually meet, so they appear to come from a point between the lens and the focus — a virtual, erect, diminished image, regardless of object position. ▥ 17.1–17.3 Spherical Lenses, Lensmaker & Power  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Converging vs Diverging Lens Sign Convention (Cartesian) Quick Chart Lensmaker's Formula & Power PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: Concave: always virtual, erect, diminished (between F and lens).

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the lens formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.
theoryItems.answer: For a thin convex lens with paraxial rays, using similar triangles from the principal rays (one parallel, one through the centre) gives u/v = (f)/(v−f) → (v−f)/v = f/u → 1/u + 1/v = 1/f.
theoryItems.example: Valid for small angles near the axis.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the lensmaker's formula.
theoryItems.answer: For a thin lens in air, summing the refraction at the two spherical surfaces (first: (n−1)/R₁, second: −(n−1)/R₂) gives 1/f = (n−1)[1/R₁ − 1/R₂]. It links focal length to refractive index and the two radii.
theoryItems.example: More curved (smaller R) or higher n → shorter f.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. State the lens formula and the sign convention.
theoryItems.answer: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (Cartesian, distances from the optical centre). u negative on the incident side; f positive for a converging (convex) lens, negative for a diverging (concave) lens. Magnification m = −v/u.
theoryItems.example: A real image has v>0, m<0.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T4. Compare a magnifying glass, a microscope and a telescope.
theoryItems.answer: Magnifying glass: magnifies a nearby object (angular, M = D/f). Microscope: magnifies a very small near object by two stages (M = L/f_o × D/f_e, very large). Telescope: magnifies distant objects (M = f_o/f_e, moderate). Each serves a different distance/scale.
theoryItems.shortcut: Magnifier: near small; Microscope: very small near; Telescope: far.
theoryItems.example: The magnification formulas differ by design.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain the power of a lens and the power of a lens combination.
theoryItems.answer: Power P = 1/f (f in metres), in dioptres; positive for converging, negative for diverging. Two thin lenses in contact have combined power P_total = P₁ + P₂, and for two separated lenses P_total = P₁+P₂ − P₁P₂d/f₁f₂.
theoryItems.example: Spectacle correction uses the right total power.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain the simple (convex) magnifying glass and angular magnification.
theoryItems.answer: A simple microscope holds an object within the focal length so the eye sees an enlarged virtual image at the near point D. Angular magnification M = D/f (image at infinity) or M = 1 + D/f (image at the near point).
theoryItems.shortcut: M = D/f or 1 + D/f ; D = 25 cm.
theoryItems.example: A 5 cm lens gives M = 6× at the near point.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the compound microscope and its magnification.
theoryItems.answer: A compound microscope uses a short-focal-length objective to form a real, magnified intermediate image, which a long-focal-length eyepiece magnifies further. The total magnification is M = (L/f_o)(1 + D/f_e) (image at near point) or M = (L/f_o)(D/f_e) (image at infinity).
theoryItems.example: Gives hundreds to thousands of times magnification.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain the astronomical telescope (image at infinity).
theoryItems.answer: An astronomical telescope uses a long-focal-length objective to form a real image at its focus, then a short-focal-length eyepiece views it. The angular magnification is M = f_o/f_e; to see stars it is adjusted so the final image is at infinity (tube length ≈ f_o + f_e).

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T9. Explain the terrestrial telescope and why it is longer.
theoryItems.answer: A terrestrial telescope inverts the astronomical image with an additional erecting lens (or prism), and because of this extra lens it needs a longer tube: tube length = f_o + f_e + 4f″ (f″ = the erecting lens focal length), so it is longer and gives lower magnification than an equal-diameter astronomical telescope.
theoryItems.shortcut: Adding an erector lens increases the tube length.
theoryItems.example: Used to see ground objects upright.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T10. A compound microscope has objective f_o = 0.5 cm and eyepiece f_e = 2 cm, tube L = 15 cm. Find magnification (image at infinity).

▣ 17.1–17.3 Spherical Lenses, Lensmaker & Power
Q1. State the lens formula and sign convention.

Answer:  For a thin lens: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (Cartesian sign convention). Distances measured from the optical centre: object distance u negative if on the incident side; f positive for a convex (converging) lens, negative for a concave (diverging) lens.
⚡ Shortcut:  1/f = 1/v + 1/u ; converging f>0, diverging f<0.
Example:  u = −2f → v = −2f (image at C, real).
Q2. Write the lensmaker's formula and explain its terms.

Answer:  1/f = (n−1)[1/R₁ − 1/R₂], where n is the relative refractive index and R₁, R₂ are the radii of curvature of the two surfaces (positive/negative per sign convention). It links focal length to material and curvature.
⚡ Shortcut:  1/f = (n−1)(1/R₁−1/R₂); more curved or higher n → shorter f.
Example:  A biconvex lens with R₁=+R, R₂=−R gives 1/f = 2(n−1)/R.
Q3. Define the power of a lens and its SI unit.
Answer:  Power P = 1/f (f in metres), measured in dioptres (D). For convex P>0, for concave P<0. The power of two thin lenses in contact adds: P_total = P₁ + P₂.
⚡ Shortcut:  P = 1/f(m); in D; add powers for thin-lens combinations.
Example:  A 20 cm convex lens → P = +5 D.
Q4. Find the focal length and power of a double-convex lens with R₁ = R₂ = 20 cm, n = 1.5.
⚡ Shortcut:  1/f = (n−1)(1/R₁−1/R₂) ; P = 1/f.
Example:  f = 20 cm, P = +5 D.
Q5. Explain a magnifying glass (simple microscope) and angular magnification M = 1 + D/f.

Answer:  A simple microscope (magnifying glass) holds an object within the near-point focal distance f, producing a virtual erect image at the near-point D. The angular magnification is M = D/f (image at infinity) or M = 1 + D/f (image at the near-point D = 25 cm).
⚡ Shortcut:  M = 1 + D/f for near-point viewing; D/f for infinity.
Example:  f = 5 cm, D = 25 cm → M = 6×.
Q6. A compound microscope with objective f_o = 0.5 cm and eyepiece f_e = 2 cm. Estimate magnification when image at infinity.
Answer:  For an image at infinity, M ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e), with L ≈ 15 cm tube length, D = 25 cm: M ≈ (15/0.5)(25/2) = 30×12.5 = 375×.
⚡ Shortcut:  M ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e) (image at infinity).
Example:  ≈ 375× magnification.
Q7. Define magnification of a lens and state its sign convention.
Answer:  Linear magnification m = h'/h = −v/u. A negative m means the image is inverted; positive m means it is erect. The magnitude |m| is the size ratio image/object.
⚡ Shortcut:  m = −v/u ; sign: + = erect, − = inverted.
Example:  An object at 2f gives m = −1 (same size, inverted).
Q8. Find the image position for an object 15 cm in front of a convex lens of f = 10 cm.

Answer:  Use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (magnitudes, convex lens): 1/v = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm (real, on the opposite side). Magnification m = v/u = 30/15 = 2, so the image is real, inverted and 2× the object size.
⚡ Shortcut:  1/v = 1/f − 1/u ; m = v/u. Object between f and 2f gives an image beyond 2f, magnified.
Example:  Image 30 cm from the lens, m = −2 (inverted, 2×).
Q9. How do you find the combined power of two thin lenses in contact?
Answer:  The powers simply add: P_total = P₁ + P₂ (each P = 1/f in metres). This is the basis of correcting the eye's vision with spectacle lenses of the right total power.
⚡ Shortcut:  P_total = P₁ + P₂ ; D = m⁻¹.
Example:  +4 D and −1 D in contact give +3 D.
Q10. Explain why a concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.

Answer:  A concave (diverging) lens spreads rays; the refracted rays diverge and never actually meet, so they appear to come from a point between the lens and the focus — a virtual, erect, diminished image, regardless of object position.
⚡ Shortcut:  Concave: always virtual, erect, diminished (between F and lens).
Example:  Used to correct myopia (short-sightedness).

⚡ Short / exam line:  M = f_o/f_e ; f_o > f_e.
Example:  Eyepiece magnifies the objective's image.

Answer:  A terrestrial telescope inverts the astronomical image with an additional erecting lens (or prism), and because of this extra lens it needs a longer tube: tube length = f_o + f_e + 4f″ (f″ = the erecting lens focal length), so it is longer and gives lower magnification than an equal-diameter astronomical telescope.

Example:  Used to see ground objects upright.
